speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, if you're creative and you have talent, that helps.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: All right, today's April 24th. We're in Sandpoint at the Pine Tree. We're talking to Irene Cook, who is the owner or co-owner of the Pine Tree, and we'd like to get some of her personal background and how she happened to be in Sandpoint. And we'll start out by saying how long have you lived in Sandpoint?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Okay, we lived here for six years. It's actually over, just days, a little over actually, six years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When you came from?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: From Santa Cruz, California.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What was in your mind when you decided to come to Idaho?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Okay, my husband worked for Park Davis, pharmaceutical sales down there, and we had a real nice home in Aptos. And about that time, the university moved in there and there was a lot of problems going on. And taxes were really going high, and we were thinking of starting a family. We didn't want to raise a family in that type of environment. It was a fast pace of life also, and so we decided to sell our home and we purchased an Airstream house trailer. And we didn't know where we would move or anything, we just started out in it. And we spent about eight months visiting the Northwest and also up into Canada, looking for a possible place to live. And we spent an awful lot of time up in Canada, especially over on the island. And finally we came back through Spokane and we had a friend in Spokane that had moved up who was a pharmacist in Spokane. We wanted to visit him. We did, and we thought while we were in Spokane we'll take a day and just drive up through the Corn Lane area and north and look it over. We did, and we spent about four days instead of one day, and we purchased 50 acres just north of town here. So we went back to California and then we decided, we still didn't know if we wanted to move up here or not, because our property was on approved property, which is land. And then we couldn't believe how the difference between California and Idaho had just been gone that long. So we decided to come back up and purchase a house near our property and to purchase an old house and to fix it up and resell it again. And then eventually get enough money to move out our property, and that's what brought us back up. We purchased this old house that was actually abandoned, and it was in real bad repair. And we bought it for almost nothing. And my husband and I spent eight months remodeling it. We parked our Airstream out back here and lived in it while we worked on the house ourselves. And we just actually gutted it all out and started all over from scratch again, almost the house. In fact, all the windows were broken and the pipes were frozen. We moved rooms around and plumbing around and made your overall on the house.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you invested quite a lot of energy and mostly more energy than money and a lot of time in it. But it was worth it to you for what your values and the things you wanted that were up here. And it is a better place to raise children. Right. So you must not regret any of it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What is your background? Had you grown up in California?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right. I was raised on the Apple Ranch.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So your people must have come to California early.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My great-grandparents on my father's side moved down to California. And then on my mother's side, her people all from England. And they just moved over from there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So it's kind of, you see a continuity there. Maybe people with the same values are getting out. Your ancestors with those values came early. And then California has kind of changed. So if you have inherited those same things, you're looking and come to Idaho. So there might be a relationship there, a continuing of the same thing. You have one sister and a brother. Yes. Are they similar to you? Where are they?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They're in California. My brother is working with my dad on the Apple Orchard. My folks still have the Apple Orchard and doing very well with it. And my sister has her own family and is working in an office.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your husband get back into pharmacy or did he try to?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no. So after we moved up here, we spent most of our energy and our money on the house, hoping to get it fixed up and eventually start a store in here. And we ran out of money. And so he decided to go out in the middle of winter and to get a job. And he wanted to get back into his old field, which there were financial openings, but not at that exact time. So he took a job for a while with a gas company driving truck. And about five months after, he had a bad accident. So he's been totally disabled from that time on.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So it was rather fortunate.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was fortunate we had the shop. In fact, we just started it when he had his accident.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you make resistance from the people in the area when you came in?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not really.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Has that situation changed? If you were coming now, would that be different?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It actually deepened. It actually deepened. It depends. I think it depends on a person's attitude. If you're swarmed towards the people, I don't think there's much resentment. But if you start acting like you're a little bit better than they are, I can understand their point, really.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How do you feel about more people coming from California now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Wish they'd stay down there. Starting to fill it up and bring up all their problems up to Idaho.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you have one son.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: One son.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you want more?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not right now with the store.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You went to high school and you had some college. You were mostly in art and crafts.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I didn't study hardly any art. I didn't study hardly any art in high school. I just picked it up on my own. And then after high school, I took private lessons. That's how I started, basically. And college, I took mostly courses like anthropology and psychology and those types of things instead of art.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you find many people up here like you with similar values? Have you made friends? Yes. You don't feel isolated or alienated or anything? Do you miss anything from the big city? Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We miss the culture.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you go to the Bocanes or that kind of thing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Once in a while.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you see anything changing? That there's a movement coming back, coming to Sandpoint with any of those things or any way to develop it here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, yes, very definitely. In fact, when we moved here, we were the first art store. And now after we've been here, there's many artists, craftsmen moving in, which I think is really good. There's lots of potters coming in and those type of people.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does it appear to make the life better for the people who were living here originally? Are they interested in that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think so.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So that they're getting some of this expansion.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right, it helps them to expose them to this, and I think it broadens their scopes a little bit.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So it makes life better for them by having the people come in. You're into the natural foods and appreciating that kind of thing too.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, in fact, if I don't buy anything in the store that's already made, I make everything from scratch.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We might mention that before you start talking to us, you put bread in the oven.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So I make our own yogurt, I make our own butter. We buy our own raw milk and make our own ice cream, make our own cheeses. I sprout all the time. I sprout instead of buying lettuce and stuff from the store. We raise our own garden. Then instead of canning, my husband does a lot of drying. We dry our own vegetables and fruits and herbs and stuff. We also make our own beef jerky. He dries that. I make our own granola, breads. We grind our own... We grind our own flours. Then I also make fresh carrot juice or whatever every day.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's almost as if it's a subsistence economy you've got going here. You can do it all right here at home.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I feel it's very economical and we don't have doctor bills or anything. It really pays off and I've got more stamina to work in the store. Many people ask how I have all this extra... How do I squeeze it in my busy schedule, which is a problem, but I feel if I'm feeling good, then I have more time to do more things.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You must be meeting a lot of your psychological and emotional needs at the same time. It keeps you energized. Right.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And it also helped with... Go ahead. Him also. I had... He was like...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, Irene stopped to put her bread in the oven, so we're back asking questions again.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was starting to mention about the little boy Hans. I had him by now to childbirth, which pays off. I was busy running the store and I started going into labor. I went to the hospital. My husband's not able to drive, so I drove him over to the hospital. I had Hans just an hour after I got there. We stayed there for three hours and I drove home with the little boy and my husband back home. Then I was back running the store just a couple days later. That's fantastic.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm glad you put that in and told about that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He's never been to a doctor.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you prepared then during your pregnancy for this type of a delivery. You're convinced it's the best way to go.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right, right. I do yoga. I work on it every day faithfully. I jog every morning. It's a mile, mile and a half every morning. We're also into transcendental meditation. I do that also morning and evening. It helps to calm your nerves and release stress. It really pays off.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm going to trade places with somebody else now so they can ask questions I know they have. Do you want to move up? I might move up here so it's on the right.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The only question I have is how does your lifestyle differ from in California?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you do all this in California? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In fact, in California, this is the reason why I got into this. My health was really in a real bad state. I was visiting the doctors all the time and getting worse and worse. My speech was really bad and I just felt horrible in California.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So it's just a healthier outlook.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's just a healthier outlook by switching my diet. It didn't happen overnight. I had to do an awful lot of studying on my own. When you're this bad of health, you don't get better overnight. You have to work at it. So it really pays off. You look really healthy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Are you convincing other people here or do you try?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, it's not really convincing. But I like to help other people too. You know?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Lily? Well, the one thing that I wanted to ask is you had mentioned the fact that you were raised on an apple farm. Now, undoubtedly, I'm almost positive that there were sprays and things connected there.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, still are.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It still are. Okay, this is what I was wondering about. Do you contribute some of your ill health to this? How does the rest of your family feel about this and this sort of thing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Maybe there's a slight factor in that with the sprays. My mom is a good cook. And she believes in cooking, you know, with basic foods and a balanced meals. But I found with my mom, she always overcooked everything. You know, we ate a lot of starches and sweets, which we didn't know about. And mom is not into natural foods at all. And my folks, their health is going downhill very badly now. They're in their 50s, you know. And my sister, who is younger than I am, who doesn't believe in natural foods, her health is just going downhill really bad too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: With the example that they have seen and the change they've seen in you, does this have any effect upon what they do?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It has slightly, but you know how families are. They'd rather take it from an outsider than someone in the family. Yeah. But they are making some changes, I can see this. I was just going to ask what your family thought of your new life. And were they upset when you left California? I think so. I think so. Because we were the only ones out of my family and my husband's family to leave. Had they been up here? Yes. They came to the United States. Right. Yeah. Now how did you learn? I know you said you took art lessons to learn some painting and so forth. How did you get into doing all the things that you do homemade in the kitchen? I mean, turning your own butter and making your own ice cream and grinding your own wheat. Mostly I just picked it up on my own from books and stuff. Because I started out on a Dale Davis' book. I don't know if you know her books. And that's what got me started on to natural foods. And then from there I started reading other books and reading about how they made butter and yogurt. And then I started doing this on my own.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You didn't make butter and this sort of thing in your home when you were growing up? No. No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We always purchased our milk from the store. Pasteurized milk and all this type of thing. What do you do with the raw milk before you drink it? Can you drink it that way? Yes. Uh-huh. So why do you buy the raw milk versus the homemade milk? The pasteurized milk has been heated or they've destroyed most of the vitamins and especially the enzymes in it. Whereas your raw milk, none of this has been destroyed. That's the difference.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Are you interested in the women's movement? Are you into that very much?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you mean these women's lib? Uh-huh. Yes and no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. Would you like to explain to me?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. It's actually, it's actually I've got mixed emotions on it. I feel that possibly these women have been held down, you know, a certain amount in this type of thing. And as I can understand their points of view on it, you know. But then I also know who's been behind them and the people that are behind them. I'm not for them at all, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, you can say that as being.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You can tell that it's what they're trying to do like they've done in many countries is to divide the people. Like they tried it here was to divide the blacks and whites and try to start a revolution with these whites and blacks. And then working on this now through the women's movement trying to divide the, in a certain way the women will put a split what I think is in the families. And this I'm against actually. And most all of your countries that have done any studying at all where this communism has taken over. They've always divided the people. It doesn't matter if it's white or black or if it's landowner against land tillers, whatever it is. There's always a division there and then that's when they come in and put in more government controls and then you have problems.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you'd be one that would say that ERA would bring more equal rights amendments, would bring more government controls.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Definitely, definitely.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And that would be a benefit.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right, so I'm against it. And still I'm all for if a woman does the job that a male does I think this woman ought to have equal pay and the whole bit. I'm for as many of the things that they're aiming for but I don't believe in what the actual end result might eventually end up becoming.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So there's a possibility of more government control. Which would in a way be related to land use planning.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right, right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you think about that issue?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because I'm also against it too because it's government controls. What it is is government is actually telling you what you can do with your property and it will eventually be until where that you'll be paying taxes on your property but you won't have any say as to what you're to do with it and they could just remove you off your property.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you feel like that kind of thing should be legislated locally?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Definitely, definitely.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Rather than from the federal government. Definitely. So you do believe in land planning?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, if it's on a local level. See this is a problem we're getting into. Whereas in the old days we actually had individual states and then each state had its own, within each state you had your own individual county governments or city governments. And if a city or county government legislated something that you didn't like you could move into the next county. Or for example if all the counties were getting the same through the state government then you could move to a different state. But now when we have the federal government getting so big that's imposing all these powers on the states and then eventually down to the local levels there's no place to go. In fact everything's the same and we're just getting more and more government controls. In fact I believe in laws and a whole bit but I think they should be at these local level where the people have a say and know exactly what's going on. Instead of somebody back in Washington who doesn't know what's happening here in your own little area trying to tell you. For example just how many carrots you can raise on your property or this type of thing. Can you see the role of women changing? Yes definitely. I think women are becoming more involved and much more creative which I think is good.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So they're not following the accepted role. If they do like you and get in touch with your own feelings and think for yourself and somehow you're free to try something different. So that's an advantage. And to the degree that they do that it's a benefit. But would you say that in the women's movement if they could go the direction of everyone having to be like what the women's livers expect it would be just reacting.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So what?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Actually I feel that the real hard core women's livers are basically probably anti-male maybe that's the wrong expression but I think basically they're out to destroy the family unit which was so basic in building up this country. This is my opinion really.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well certainly you at this time particularly your husband needs your support a lot.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right, right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you've exhibited a lot of strength and staying with it and your ideas I see. Right. You're bringing your family through a hard time. Did you feel that your husband supported you when you were in ill health and this sort of thing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, yeah. I'm just going to see something I can't. Oh, this is also where I think it's important that women do get out and improve themselves and get a good education and also try to better themselves because an emergency might come up where they'll have to rely on it. And so I feel that we're in a woman in the times past many times has been held down where she's had to stay in the home which I can see advantages also to that too but there's also disadvantages because now in this day and age if anything happened to her husband and she's not skilled what's this woman going to do?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And it certainly is easy to see that in your life. Yeah, yeah. It's fortunate that you had the strength and the flexibility to take on something else.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What do women in standpoint do? Do they get divorced or widowed or do they get menial jobs if they aren't skilled? Many of them do I guess probably as maids or waitresses or however which is you know it's we need those type of people we need the jobs done you know and there's a real need for it but still I think women wouldn't prove herself to you know which would be also easier on her wouldn't have to. Because work is hard and get better pay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well I would like to continue to talk to you some more but we are you know we do have to go check out of our motel. I would like to continue this we're hoping to come up here again sometime.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Okay, great.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And I feel really lucky to have been able to talk to her. And for you to take your time off your work. Oh that's okay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. Actually it's my pleasure really.
